That keeps support under Australian short-end yields and should limit downside for the Australian dollar on soft domestic data. Fuel is the key transmis
articles.content: Westpac's call for a November follow-up hike, despite the sentiment slump, signals that inflation risk still outweighs demand weakness for the RBA. That keeps support under Australian short-end yields and should limit downside for the Australian dollar on soft domestic data. Fuel is the key transmission channel, so further gains in crude prices would sharpen both the inflation pressure and the squeeze on consumers. The risk for markets is that a rate-hiking central bank meets a household sector already at recession-level gloom, raising the odds of a sharper slowdown in consumer spending into 2027. --- Australian households took one look at the RBA's latest hike and sent sentiment to recession-era lows, yet Westpac reckons the central bank isn't finished. Summary: The Westpac-Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment Index fell 4.7% to 80.4 in October from 84.4. Sentiment dropped to 67.2 among those surveyed after the RBA hike, a level previously seen only in the early 1990s recession. The cash rate is at 4.6%, the highest since 2011, and petrol is back above $2.30 a litre. Just over 80% of post-decision respondents expect mortgage rates to rise further over the next year. Westpac still expects the RBA to hike again at its November 2–3 meeting, citing fuel costs flowing into broader prices and AI-driven demand pressures. Australian consumer sentiment slumped in October after the Reserve Bank of Australia's latest rate hike, with the Westpac-Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment Index falling 4.7% to 80.4 from 84.4 in September. The reading ranks among the 40 weakest since the monthly survey began in the early 1970s. Westpac said this year has already produced two other readings in that group, in April and June, marking the worst stretch of persistently weak sentiment since the early 1990s recession. Pessimists outnumbered optimists in 102 of the 106 population groups the survey tracks. The RBA decision appears to have had an immediate effect. Among respondents surveyed before the announcement, sentiment was 86.9, slightly up on September. Among those surveyed afterwards, it plunged to 67.2, a level previously seen in complete surveys only during the depths of the early 1990s recession. The gap of nearly 20% between the two groups is the largest since Westpac began tracking daily responses in 2019. The macro backdrop explains the pressure. The latest hike took the cash rate to 4.6%, its highest since 2011, and Westpac expects the standard variable mortgage rate to rise above 9% for the first time since 2008. At the same time, national average petrol prices have climbed back above $2.30 a litre, close to April's peak and up almost 25% since the start of the year, as the energy shock from the Middle East conflict continues to hit household budgets. Consumers expect more of the same. The survey's mortgage rate expectations index rose 5.5% to just below its May peak, and among those surveyed after the RBA decision, just over 80% expect mortgage rates to rise further over the next year, up from 63% in September. Concerns about jobs are also creeping higher, with the unemployment expectations index now clearly above its long-run average, though still well short of past peaks. Westpac described consumers as on edge rather than alarmed. Westpac said consumers' worries still centre mainly on the cost of living and interest rates rather than the job losses and insolvencies typical of a recession. Despite the sentiment hit, Westpac expects the RBA to raise rates again at its next meeting on November 2 and 3. It said higher fuel costs are starting to feed into prices across a wider range of goods and services, a sign that upside inflation risks flagged by the central bank are materialising, while the board is also wary of demand pressures from the AI and data centre investment boom. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: QuikStor and KISS Integrate to Make Portfolio-Wide Smart Access Finally Practical
articles.desc: /PRNewswire-PRWeb/ -- QuikStor, the modern AI-powered SaaS operating platform for the self-storage industry, and Keep It Simple Storage (KISS), the creator of...
articles.content: QuikStor and KISS Integrate to Make Portfolio-Wide Smart Access Finally Practical QuikStor's native integration with Keep It Simple Storage (KISS) connects battery-free NFC smart access directly to the tenant record. No WiFi at the door, no gateways to maintain, and no manual steps required. /PRNewswire-PRWeb/ -- QuikStor, the modern AI-powered SaaS operating platform for the self-storage industry, and Keep It Simple Storage (KISS), the creator of the battery-free, NFC-powered ONELock smart access system, today announced a native integration connecting QuikStor Management Software directly to the KISS access control platform. The integration means access follows the tenant record automatically. When a tenant moves in through QuikStor, access is granted, When an account goes delinquent, access is restricted. And when an overlock is placed, it's placed. There are no manual steps, a separate system to log into, or WiFI required at the door. Smart access control has long been one of the most compelling operational upgrades available to self-storage operators. It eliminates manual lock checks, automates overlocking, and gives tenants a modern, keyless experience from gate to unit. The barrier to adoption industry-wide? Infrastructure. Traditional smart lock and access control systems require WiFi at the door, Bluetooth gateways, hardwired connections, or ongoing maintenance overhead that makes portfolio-wide rollout cost-prohibitive for independent operators. KISS was designed to remove every one of those roadblocks. KISS's ONELock is battery-free and doesn't need WiFi or gateways to maintain. It runs on NFC, which means a tenant's phone is the key. Operators can complete a facility rollout in less than half a day. For a multi-site portfolio, that changes the math on smart access entirely. When connected to QuikStor, the KISS platform gives operators a single place to manage units, gates, doors, and tenant access, all in step with the tenant record they're already running. "Smart access control at the unit level has always been the right idea, but the infrastructure requirements made it impractical for most operators at scale. KISS solves that problem," says Tony Gardner, Vice President of Strategic Relationships for QuikStor. "QuikStor connects the access layer directly to the tenant record. Together, the two platforms make portfolio-wide smart access achievable for any size of operator." What the QuikStor + KISS Integration Does When the QuikStor and KISS platforms are linked, the tenant record automatically drives access by its status: move-ins trigger immediate access, delinquency triggers restriction based on operator-defined rules, and overlocks are triggered without a staff member having to walk the facility. Even more, every access event is logged and visible inside your FMS. "From day one, our goal at KISS has been to make smart access simple enough and affordable enough to deploy across an entire portfolio—not just at a handful of showcase properties," said Robert Kapp, Founder and CEO of Keep It Simple Storage. "This integration with QuikStor takes that vision another step forward. The tenant record drives everything automatically, while our battery-free NFC technology eliminates the WiFi, gateways, wiring, batteries, and infrastructure that have traditionally made smart access difficult and expensive to scale. Together, we're giving operators a simpler way to automate access from the gate all the way to the individual unit." QuikStor is the modern SaaS operating platform for the self-storage industry, built by operators, for operators. QuikStor delivers a fast, reliable, purpose-built facility management system designed to power intelligent automation and streamlined operations, giving operators the confidence, performance, and long-term partner they need to scale. articles.title: Fast food chains' credibility problem
articles.desc: The Bottom Line: This week’s edition of the weekly restaurant finance newsletter looks at the strange fallout from a report on McDonald’s use of AI, and what it says about chains’ credibility.
articles.content: California fines The Kickin' Crab for selling unregistered franchises McDonald's is fending off suggestions that AI sets its prices. | Photo by Jonathan Maze This is from the weekly restaurant finance newsletter The Bottom Line. To get this in your inbox every Monday morning, McDonald’s has a credibility problem right now, and so does the fast-food sector. The Chicago-based giant was subject of a report in Reuters about the use of AI in its pricing recommendation. The report, and much of the reaction, conflated the use of AI in a pricing recommendation tool with the use of AI to set prices. All our sources, including the company and its operators, steadfastly maintained that McDonald’s only uses the tool to recommend prices , and that franchisees are the ones who make the determination. Franchisees often don’t follow the recommendations, much to the chagrin of company executives. It didn’t necessarily matter on social media. More than a few commenters on our posts said the company was flat-out lying. Our feed was filled with debates between some operators and customers convinced that McDonald’s uses AI to set prices, and that it employs dynamic pricing, meaning it raises or lowers prices based on demand and time of day. Much of this is rooted in mistrust of AI, especially when it comes to pricing. And plenty of industries, like airlines, use the technology to adjust prices all the time. Consumers also loathe the concept of dynamic pricing and push back hard on any industry that does it. These reactions are understandable. Fast-food chains could probably benefit in some capacity from dynamic pricing, but are skittish about it, for this very reason. After this, and a previous incident involving Wendy’s, no executive in their right mind would go forward with a public pronouncement about dynamic pricing anytime soon. But the bigger issue here may simply be the fast-food sector’s credibility. Consumers are ready to believe that McDonald’s will do dynamic pricing because it’s a big company and they are frustrated generally about prices. This frustration extends to much of the broader sector. Not only are they ready to believe the worst when it comes to pricing, they refuse to change their perception when presented with evidence to the contrary. Maybe that’s a broader social media problem. But it’s an issue that the fast-food sector is going to have to overcome in the coming years. We published an extensive look into Crumbl , where stores are closing and the company is laying off workers. The chain’s challenges have exposed some of the franchise’s more unique requirements, notably the way it uses in-store cameras. Chip City shut down despite multiple funding rounds . This is a bad time to be a cookie concept, apparently. Another wild story comes courtesy of Subway , where the longtime former CEO of the nonprofit Independent Purchasing Cooperative was indicted in connection with an $80 million bribery scheme. this inside look at the McDonald’s archive , one of the cooler things I’ve seen on the beat. Two other leftovers from our coverage of McDonald’s Investor Day: The company has low expectations for fast-food sector growth. the company is getting into the advertising business. The K-shaped economy is a big reason for this , and it doesn’t appear to be getting any better. Crumbl’s average-unit volumes were still over $1 million last year, but they’ve been trending downward. They’ve been worse this year, according to franchisees. “At the end of the day, I’m the CEO and the buck stops with me. It’s my fault where we are today.” -Jason McGowan, Crumbl’s CEO and cofounder, to franchisees. I wrote a lot about McDonald’s. And the K-shaped economy. But even that mentions McDonald’s. articles.title: Dave's Hot Chicken says the future of delivery will be automated
articles.desc: Dave’s CTO Leon Davoyan talks about why the brand is going all-in on robot and drone delivery at the FSTEC conference.
articles.content: Dave's Hot Chicken says the future of delivery will be automated How Scooter's Coffee solved a delivery management emergency With text-to-order, DoorDash moves beyond the app 'The Thinking Machine' author gives optimistic view of AI, with guardrails Wonder details its plans for an autonomous food platform Dave’s Hot Chicken wants more drones and robots delivering its food. The chain is testing the technology in select locations, including a drone delivery test set to launch in California soon. In the future, it plans to fulfill all orders placed through its mobile app or website with a drone or a wheeled robot. This experience is better for the customer, in part because it’s faster, especially with drones, CTO Leon Davoyan said during an interview at the FSTEC conference in September. “Long gone are gonna be the days of you getting soggy food or french fries that are not hot and not as crispy,” he said. “It's gonna be a game changer.” Drone delivery will have to clear several hurdles before it can become mainstream. There are FAA regulations and payload limitations. And there will be tech needed to connect the dots between restaurants, drone providers, and customers. But Davoyan believes these issues can be solved as early as next year. Dave’s wants to be ready when that happens, so that it doesn’t have to learn drone delivery on the fly (no pun intended). articles.title: Tories Cautious on Inheritance Tax Cut Amid Fiscal Constraints
articles.desc: Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith highlights need for a fiscally responsible plan before cutting inheritance tax, while Kemi Badenoch hints at moral justification for tax reform.
articles.content: Tories Cautious on Inheritance Tax Cut Amid Fiscal Constraints | Politics Pick countries on the world map and get breaking news alerts in your browser — free, no app. Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith highlights need for a fiscally responsible plan before cutting inheritance tax, while Kemi Badenoch hints at moral justification for tax reform. At the opening session of the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham, senior officials offered a cautious look at the future of UK under a potential return to government by the Tories. In a televised interview with Sky News, Andrew Griffith, the party's shadow chancellor, admitted that the Conservatives do not yet have the means to eliminate the levy immediately, citing the nation's precarious fiscal position. He emphasized that any tax reform would be contingent on a clear, responsible plan for funding the changes. "The job of the chancellor is to make sure that those can be paid for," Griffith said, echoing a sentiment that the UK's public finances are the worst in history. He warned that the £28‑year‑old peak in the cost of borrowing would continue to weigh on mortgage rates and overall economic stability. Griffith added that the party's ultimate goal is to remove inheritance tax, stating that it is inherently a double or triple tax that undermines people's drive to save and pass on wealth to future generations. Yet he made it clear the plan is conditional on ensuring the public books remain balanced. The conversation came a day after party leader Kemi Badenoch, who is widely seen as a senior contender for the next prime ministerial candidacy, suggested that cutting death duties would be morally right, noting that many families feel they are taxed twice when they leave an estate to their children. Badenoch has repeatedly highlighted her willingness to abolish or significantly reduce the tax but her remarks were carefully framed around fiscal responsibility. In a Sunday Times interview, she said: "It is morally right that people don't get taxed twice. It is morally right that if you work hard and want to give something to your children the government doesn't take it away. " She added that the party will not announce tax cuts unless they can demonstrate funding plans. The current inheritance tax regime levies 40 per cent on estates valued over £325,000, although the effective rate is often closer to 25 per cent because of transferability of allowances and a £350,000 main home exemption that effectively raises the threshold for married couples to roughly £1 million. The tax is largely seen as aimed at wealth redistribution, and while the majority of households never pay it, it remains a political touchstone. Around the same time, there were murmurs that the Tory leadership was weighing a broader agenda that would push for sharp reductions in both taxing the wealthy and boosting public spending. However, Griffith's remarks suggest that the party may shift its focus to building a balanced budget first, before revisiting tax cuts. He pointed out that the current government's borrowing costs, already the highest in 28 years, would force any pragmatic policy to include "ways to pay for it" in order to prevent a further worsening of public debt. In this context, Griffith stressed that even though the party wants to abolish inheritance tax on a moral foundation, any such plan must be paired with a robust fiscal framework. He reiterated that the Conservatives' policy proposals concerning the national debt, tax burden, and borrowing interest will have direct implications for consumers the next year, especially as mortgage rates are projected to rise with the economy's debt profile. The conference itself saw other policy signals, including a renewed emphasis on the role of Parliament to protect taxpayers from double or triple taxation. articles.desc: The final day's trading has been announced for the former WH Smith in Didcot
articles.content: Final day announced for town's former WH Smith | Herald Series Final day announced for town's former WH Smith This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. The final day's trading has been announced for the former WH Smith store in Didcot. The branch of TG Jones, formerly WH Smith in Broadway, is part of the company's restructuring which will see its total number of High Street stores drastically cut back. The Didcot shop, featuring a branch post office, is just one of 150 TG Jones stores set to close in the plan, which could result in the loss of hundreds of jobs. READ MORE: Hundreds gather at model railway show The final day's trading is expected to be January 9, 2027. Didcot and Wantage MP Olly Glover has written to the new Small Business Minister, Lord Leong, calling for urgent action to address worsening access to Post Office services across Didcot and Wantage following the confirmed closure of the TG Jones Didcot Post Office branch. The letter to the new minister follows a long-running campaign led by the MP to protect local Post Office services, including a parliamentary petition presented earlier this year opposing the closure of East Hagbourne Post Office. More than 175 residents signed the parliamentary petition, while a separate community petition attracted over 1,100 signatures. The closure of East Hagbourne Post Office removed access to essential services including postal services, banking facilities and government services. At the time, the Government argued that alternative branches remained available nearby, in the response to the petition. Mr Glover warned ministers in July that this position was unsustainable, citing uncertainty surrounding the future of Didcot Post Office and existing capacity pressures at Georgetown Post Office in Wantage Road, including long queues and unexpected closures. This letter received no response from the Government. Now that the TG Jones branch has now been confirmed as closing, residents in a town of approximately 37,000 people will be left relying on a single branch, Georgetown Post Office, that is already under significant strain. Mr Glover has released a petition entitled 'Save Didcot's Post Office Services'. He said: “The removal of the Post Office in East Hagbourne, and now Didcot's TG Jones branch, is only going to increase the pressure on our local infrastructure. "I warned the Government of this back in July, and received no response. I really hope that Minister Leong will take this seriously and ensure that residents in my constituency are able to access the basic services that we need.” District councillor Crispin Topping said: "East Hagbourne has lost a vital part of our community. The Post Office served the Hagbournes and neighbouring villages for more than 20 years, and we are devastated to see it go. With the closure of the Didcot TG Jones store, local residents are now facing a real Post Office crisis. It's time the Government took this seriously." Didcot West district councillor Tony Worgan said: "Didcot is a thriving town with a rapidly growing population. The closure of local Post Office branches is the complete opposite of what Didcot residents need right now. "What is needed is reliable, accessible infrastructure to support residents' everyday needs - not to send them to branches miles away." articles.title: Urbane Café prepares for growth outside California with a slow-and-steady pace
articles.desc: This fast-casual chain did not take the private-equity route for expansion. Nearing 50 units, CEO Tom Holt has no regrets.
articles.content: Urbane Café prepares for growth outside California with a slow-and-steady pace Goop Kitchen co-CEO on growth ahead for actress Gwyneth Paltrow's restaurant brand Pura Vida Miami captures health-minded diners with fast-casual hybrid A Chimichurri Steak sandwich at Urbane Cafe on house-made focaccia. |Photo courtesy of Urbane Cafe Averaging a 20% growth rate over two decades may not be the sexiest of business stories, but it’s certainly an enviable one in the fast-casual space. That’s according to Tom Holt, president and CEO of Urbane Café, which opened its 45th location last month. Unit number 45 opened in the Glendale neighborhood of Los Angeles, and Urbane is planning to add two more restaurants this year, both in California. Next year, another eight or nine units are planned, and the Ventura, California-based chain is moving out of California. The concept is open in Nevada, and next year will come to Arizona. Holt said the chain is looking for sites in Utah. The goal is to hit 100 units by 2030. And all restaurants are company owned. Holt has no plans to franchise. Urbane Café’s growth comes without private-equity funding, though the chain did receive an investment in 2017 from the founders of Panda Express Andrew and Peggy Cherng have long been supporters of small growing brands. Holt described Andrew Cherng as a mentor who has helped guide Urbane’s slow-and-steady all-company-owned growth. Holt said the brand “dated” some private-equity firms early on. “But I wasn’t ready. The concept wasn’t ready. I wouldn’t know where we’d be right now [if the chain took a private-equity investment],” he said. “We’d probably have more units, but I probably wouldn’t have my seat right now.” And things are looking pretty good from Holt’s seat for Urbane Café, which has an average unit volume of $2.1 million in about 1,800-square feet. That’s exceptional compared with Jersey Mike’s ($1.4 million) and Subway ($510,000), according to Technomic data. The roughly 3,400-unit Jersey Mike's and more-than 18,000-unit Subway are both heavily franchised. Holt said Urbane Café’s same-store sales are up about 4% this year, though traffic has been flat. The cyclospora outbreak had an impact, Holt said, though Urbane Café was in no way implicated. Still, all sandwiches are served with salads. For a while, he said, “You could see guests leaving [the salads]. But now people are eating salads again.” Urbane Café is, at its core, a sandwich concept, but a more premium one. Holt founded the concept in 2003 to be a more healthful option. At the center of each restaurant is a hearth, and the chain’s signature focaccia is baked from scratch in each restaurant. That’s a real differentiator in comparison to brands like Subway or Jersey Mike’s, which bake bread in stores, but the dough is made off site. “It would be a lot easier doing a commissary or doing frozen dough,” said Holt. “But I personally eat at our restaurants every day, and my family does. And I feel strongly about offering the best quality possible.” Holt argues that Urbane Café doesn’t get enough credit for its scratch cooking. “But it’s something I feel good about, and I think our team does,” he said. “This builds into culture.” At Urbane Café, sandwiches account for about 65% of sales, but the chain added bowls about four years ago, and that category has been growing. A recently introduced Garlic Sesame Steak Bowl has become a top seller, for example — and is yet another indicator that consumers are not tired of bowls, as is often reported. s Garlic Sesame bowl. | Photo courtesy of Urbane Caf Holt is working on building Urbane Café’s catering program, which is now about 10% of sales, and he sees a real opportunity there. “We’re a little behind,” he said. “Catering is up 30% from last year, but there’s so much room to build on that.” At Urbane Café, guests order on kiosks, but there are also cashiers who are trained to add a touch of hospitality by offering assistance or giving diners the option of

articles.title: Technology transforms a centuries-old Kyoto cooking tradition into zero-waste Obanzai
articles.desc: Modern-day Obanzai Rolls are created by sushi robots but follow the same sustainability principles developed hundreds of years ago by Japanese home cooks.
articles.content: Technology transforms a centuries-old Kyoto cooking tradition into zero-waste Obanzai Chicken and cheese take the lead on menus Biscuits are at the heart of Bojangles' menu and culture How Josh Hunt is reshaping seafood at Cordelia Fishbar Zero-waste Obanzai Rolls filled with vegetables, tofu, cooked beef, and other ingredients. | Photo by Hachikin Creative Traditional Kyoto-style home cooking is based on the Japanese principle of Mottainai, the belief that ingredients and resources should be valued and used to their fullest potential. Tabletop sushi robots are now taking that age-old zero-waste ethos into the 21st century with the creation of Obanzai Rolls. The premise of Mottainai is to make sure all parts of food are used so the household will have meals for the next day. But hundreds of years ago, there was no refrigeration, so each Obanzai dish had to last a long time without that preservation equipment, explained Japanese food designer and cultural strategist Sayaka Wada at a demo hosted by robotics company Autec. “Obanzai originated in Kyoto but it’s used all over Japan now, where people think of it like soul food; mom’s meal that really warms up your heart,” she said. Typically, Obanzai dishes feature root vegetables such as taro, burdock root, or pumpkin simmered in a broth flavored with dashi or light sauce. But using Autec’s sushi robots, Wada translated these ingredients into three different Obanzai Rolls featuring pieces of cooked beef, fish, tofu, and vegetables. The sushi robot can flatten a sheet of cooked rice in seconds. | Photo by Pat Cobe Wada began with a Tofu Atsu-age Roll. When cooked rice was fed into one of the robotic machines, it formed a base for the roll in seconds. Layered on top of the nori and rice were seasoned and simmered tofu, atsu-age or deep-fried tofu, burdock root, and tamagoyaki (egg). Once those ingredients were added, another sushi robot quickly rolled it up and it was ready to eat. Next up was a Unagi Kabayaki Roll made with eel, pickled cucumbers, burdock root, and tamagoyaki (egg), followed by the Beef Shigureni Roll, a combination of simmered beef, takuan (bright yellow pickled daikon), and burdock root. While Americans are used to sushi featuring raw fish rolled up with rice and seaweed, these Obanzai use cooked, pickled, and non-perishable ingredients that conform with their zero-waste premise. But they also infused the rolls with a deeper, more savory flavor. Members help make our journalism possible. articles.title: Trade to Technology: India and Switzerland Expand Strategic Partnership With New Pacts
articles.desc: India and Switzerland signed multiple agreements covering migration, mobility, transport technology, innovation and entrepreneurship during PM Modi’s meeting with Swiss President Guy Parmelin.
articles.content: Trade to Technology: India and Switzerland Expand Strategic Partnership With New Pacts | Dynamite News Trade to Technology: India and Switzerland Expand Strategic Partnership With New Pacts Trade to Technology: India and Switzerland Expand Strategic Partnership With New Pacts India and Switzerland signed multiple agreements covering migration, mobility, transport technology, innovation and entrepreneurship during PM Modi’s meeting with Swiss President Guy Parmelin. PM Narendra Modi and Swiss President Guy Parmelin strengthen India-Switzerland ties as multiple agreements are signed on mobility, technology and innovation. (Images: X) India and Switzerland have taken steps to deepen their bilateral partnership across trade, migration, transportation, science, technology and innovation with several agreements and cooperation arrangements signed during the bilateral meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Swiss President Guy Parmelin. The discussions covered the growing economic relationship between the two countries with trade remaining a key area of engagement. The Swiss side also highlighted the first anniversary of the implementation of the Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement between India and the European Free Trade Association. Trade Pact Opens New Opportunities for India and Switzerland The Swiss leadership highlighted the mutual benefits emerging from the trade partnership between India and EFTA. India stands to gain from increased capital flows, technology transfers and improved access to international markets, particularly for high-value-added goods. Switzerland meanwhile sees India as an important and rapidly growing economic partner at a time when global trade faces increasing uncertainty. A senior Swiss economic delegation accompanied the visit, reflecting Switzerland’s interest in expanding business opportunities created by the agreement. Switzerland is also looking to advance discussions on an investment protection agreement to provide a stronger framework for future investments. Progress on intellectual property protection was also identified as an important component of the broader economic relationship. Migration and mobility emerged as another important area of India-Switzerland cooperation. During the bilateral meeting, the two sides signed an agreement related to a Migration and Mobility Partnership. The pact is aimed at strengthening structured cooperation between the two countries on migration-related matters. An agreement on the Exchange of Young Professionals was also signed, providing another institutional framework for mobility and professional exchanges between India and Switzerland. The agreements are expected to add greater depth to people-to-people and professional connections between the two countries. India and Switzerland Expand Cooperation in Transport Technology A separate memorandum of understanding was signed for the promotion and collaboration of transportation technologies, mobility systems and infrastructure in identified areas. The agreement brings together Switzerland’s expertise in transport technology with India’s large-scale infrastructure and mobility requirements. The cooperation involves Switzerland’s Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research and India’s Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. Innovation and Technology Transfer Take Centre Stage Science, technology and innovation also featured prominently in the agreements announced during the visit. A Letter of Intent was issued between India’s Department of Science and Technology and the Swiss National Science Foundation. The two sides also advanced cooperation with the Zurich University of Applied Sciences in areas including innovation, technology transfer and entrepreneurship. An implementation arrangement between the Department of Science and Technology and the Zurich University of Applied Sciences is expected to provide a framework for greater collaboration in these fields. articles.title: Nobel medicine prize goes to 3 scientists for pioneering research into brain activity
articles.desc: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel have researched light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. They are based in Germany and the United States.
articles.content: Nobel medicine prize goes to 3 scientists for pioneering research into brain activity - Anchorage Daily News Nobel medicine prize goes to 3 scientists for pioneering research into brain activity Kostya Manenkov, Lauran Neergaard, Adithi Ramakrishnan, Associated Press STOCKHOLM — The Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded Monday to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have carried out research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. The Nobel Assembly lauded their work and said their tool is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries. Deisseroth, 54, is a Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator and Stanford University professor in California. Hegemann, 71, is at Humboldt University in Berlin, and Nagel, 73, most recently worked at the University of Würzburg, also in Germany, the assembly said. Research opened a new era in neuroscience Optogenetics opened what the Nobel assembly called a new era in neuroscience following the discovery of a light-controlled switch to turn on and off nerve cells and circuits in the brain to better learn how it works. The research has started unraveling the pathways that lead to behavior and disease. The breakthrough began when Hegemann explored how a single-celled type of green algae can swim toward light. He and Nagel discovered a particular protein that, when illuminated by blue light, opens a channel to create an electrical impulse. Putting that protein into other cells makes them light-sensitive. Deisseroth then worked with the gene that controls that protein to create a light-controlled switch for nerve cells in the brains of living mice. “People usually think about light as a way of collecting information to observe things,” he said. “But this is the opposite of that. This is using light to control things, to make things happen, and to do it in a very precise way.” Deisseroth first developed tiny fibers to deliver light to cells modified with the light-sensitive gene and said there now are other techniques to switch on or off neurons being studied. Optogenetics is mostly a research technique to learn how specific neurons and neural circuits work, which can then lead to development of treatments, including regimens for autism and schizophrenia that other scientists are pursuing, he said. A technique he called direct optogenetics is being used to test a treatment for a genetic form of vision loss called retinitis pigmentosa. Technique offers window into brain activity The University of Pittsburgh’s Jeremy Berg was at the U.S. National Institutes of Health in the early 2000s when it awarded Deisseroth major funding for “this vision of optogenetics that was pretty much spot-on the way it played out.” “It’s a very precise set of tools for doing experiments about how the brain works that are pretty hard to do any other way,” Berg said. Abdel El Manira, a member of Nobel Assembly, said the impact of optogenetics goes beyond the understanding of a healthy brain. “It has also helped reveal how specific brain circuits are disrupted, with implications for conditions such as blindness, depression, addiction and dementia,” El Manira said. ”Yet despite these extraordinary advances, the brain still holds countless mysteries, with much more left to learn and discover. And optogenetics has given us a powerful means to take on these challenges.” One winner had just gone to bed when he learned of the award Deisseroth, a self-described night owl, said he was up late in his Northern California home working on papers and emailing students. He had just gone to lie down when he got the call from the Nobel Assembly. “No real sleep was achieved,” he told The Associated Press in a phone call an hour after the announcement. He said the next task on his to-do list was to pack school lunches for his children, who were still sound asleep. “That’s my one obligation I have

articles.title: Turning Data Into Decisions
articles.desc: Abigail Dirks, a senior data scientist at the Tufts Center for the Study of Drug Development, on the challenge of turning data into sound decisions in the arena of clinical research
articles.content: Friedman School of Nutrition Science and Policy Jean Mayer USDA Human Nutrition Research Center on Aging Get the latest news and stories from Tufts delivered right to your inbox. A Tufts data scientist explains how data quality, AI, and human judgment are shaping decision-making in biotechnology In clinical research, small details can have big consequences for the quality of data. Take something as simple as how soon after an event study participants make a diary entry; the longer they wait to record what happened, the less accurately they may remember it. Imprecise recollections can then become imprecise data—and that data could be used to help determine something as important as the safety or efficacy of a given treatment. For Abigail Dirks, a senior data scientist at the Tufts Center for the Study of Drug Development , this example illustrates a central challenge in clinical research. As she puts it, “Collecting data is one thing; making sure it is reliable enough to support sound decisions is another.” Dirks studies the operational side of clinical research: how trials are conducted, how different approaches affect their performance, and how data can be used to make better decisions along the way. She also teaches Data-Driven Decision-Making in Biotechnology , a self-paced course offered as part of Tufts University College’s new research and development micro-credentials in life sciences Developed with industry leaders and designed for working professionals, the self-paced micro-credentials build practical skills for life sciences careers at the intersection of science and business. In data-driven biotechnology, says Dirks, “that means understanding the quality of the data you’re using and knowing what it can—and can’t—tell you.” Dirks discusses with Tufts Now how the challenge of turning data into sound decisions plays out in practice across clinical research. What is a decision being made today with data that would have been impossible 10 or 20 years ago? I don’t know that it’s one particular decision. The bigger change is that we have so much more data available, along with much better ways to collect and manage it. That allows us to ask deeper questions and get closer to the root causes of what we’re seeing. We’re also getting better at using data proactively. Instead of simply looking back at what happened, we can sometimes use what we know to anticipate what might happen next and make decisions accordingly. In clinical research, for example, operational data can help us understand how different approaches affect the way a trial is conducted and decide which strategies might improve its performance. As biotechnology companies collect and analyze more health and genetic data, what benefits should ordinary people expect—and what trade-offs should they be aware of? The benefit is that more data can help researchers develop better treatments and move toward more personalized medicine. The tradeoff is that sharing more personal information inevitably raises questions about privacy, security, and how data will be used. There’s also the question of whose data we’re collecting. The quality of the data going in determines the quality of what we get out of it. If certain racial, ethnic, socioeconomic, or educational groups are underrepresented in clinical research, then the evidence we generate may be less representative, too. That’s why participation and representation are so important. We need high-quality data, but we also need data that reflect a broad range of people—and participants deserve transparency about what is being collected and how it will be used. What is a common misconception the public has about artificial intelligence in biotechnology? The idea of using artificial intelligence to develop medicines is not well understood by many. articles.title: Major study opens window to the brain when an emotion first appears
articles.desc: Discover the science behind emotions and how they shape our brain activity and responses to the world around us.
articles.content: Major study opens window to the brain when an emotion first appears - The Hindu Subscribed with another email? Logout and Login with that one. Account subscription benefits alongside Premium Stories, Editorials, Opinions and more. Unlock these with Subscription Major study opens window to the brain when an emotion first appears Despite being so fundamental to our survival as a species, scientists are still piecing together how emotions arise in our brains. In a study recently published in the journal , in fact, scientists have just reported mapping the brain-wide activity patterns that trigger emotions Image used for representative purposes only. | Photo Credit: notorious v1ruS/Unsplash Simply put, emotions are intangible responses to what we see happening around us. They arise spontaneously, without conscious thought. Emotions allowed early humans to efficiently dodge dangers as they explored the world around them. While the world and our lives in it are very different today than the way they were for our ancestors, our emotions haven’t changed. 2026 Nobel medicine prize: Trio wins for optogenetics work Despite being so fundamental to our survival as a species, however, scientists are still piecing together how emotions arise in our brains. In a study recently published in , in fact, scientists have just reported mapping the brain-wide activity patterns that trigger emotions. The team found that once an emotion was set off, it outlasted the trigger that sparked it in the first place. If this sounds familiar, it’s because this is what you feel when you accidentally stub your toe, burn your hand, and even when you enjoy your favourite flavour of ice cream. New low-cost MRI machine can improve access to diagnostics in India In all these examples, there is incoming sensory information that prompts an emotional response while the good or bad feeling lasts even after the body part has been reflexively pulled back or after the ice cream is finished. In the new study, scientists led by Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University examined how emotions emerged in response to unpleasant (but not painful) sensory stimuli. The participants were subjected to an eye puff assay: a machine called a tonometer blew light puffs of air into their left eye in specific sequences. Each puff lasted about 60 ms, the gap between puffs was 3-8 s long, and the entire session lasted 5 minutes. The scientists varied the gap between puffs so that participants didn’t reflexively tense up for the next puff they knew was coming. During the entire duration, a high-speed camera recorded the way participants closed their eyes and their behavioral and subjective responses. An individual in front of a tonometer. | Photo Credit: Jason7825 (CC BY-SA) As expected, repeated puffs of air to the eye elicited reflexive blinking as participants instinctively pulled back from the tonometer. They also kept the eye closed for certain durations or squinted or blinked rapidly during the gaps. As part of their subjective reports, the participants said this experience was “unpleasant” and “annoying”. The scientists recruited a separate group of participants who were, at the time of the study, inpatients at the Stanford university hospital and had electrodes planted in their brains to check for epileptic seizures. Members of this group who consented to participate underwent the same eyepuff assay. The scientists found that these participants’ behavioural responses were consistent with those of the previous group. They also blinked reflexively and kept their eyes closed for (relatively) long periods. The real story emerged in the brain activity patterns. Where does ‘us versus them’ bias in the brain come from?
